hypotheses.text: Unlike MMDS1-3 where marked hyperglycinemia is a hallmark diagnostic feature, elevations in CSF and plasma glycine in FDXR-associated MMDS9B are restricted to severe infantile-onset presentations and are absent in juvenile- or adult-onset optic-acoustic neuropathy.
hypotheses.rationale: It is critical to establish whether hyperglycinemia can reliably rule out or rule in MMDS9B. While MMDS1-3 cause severe lipoic acid-dependent glycine cleavage defects leading to prominent nonketotic hyperglycinemia, FDXR patients with milder sensory phenotypes may maintain normal glycine metabolism, whereas severe infantile FDXR cases have shown mild elevations.

evidence.text: Vanlander and Van Coster report that in FDXR deficiency, CSF lactate and to a milder extent plasma lactate was increased, which was also the case for CSF and plasma glycine in an early described cohort.

hypotheses.text: CSF and plasma lactate elevations in MMDS9B are mild and intermittent rather than constant, with cerebral lactate peaks detected on MR spectroscopy in no more than 30% of assessed individuals.
hypotheses.rationale: Differentiating MMDS9B from classic primary mitochondrial encephalopathies depends on understanding the true penetrance and stability of lactate elevation in both biofluids and the central nervous system.

hypotheses.text: Normal CSF-to-plasma glycine ratios reliably distinguish FDXR deficiency from primary glycine encephalopathy / nonketotic hyperglycinemia, even when borderline or mild elevations of absolute glycine concentrations occur in plasma or CSF.
hypotheses.rationale: Secondary or mild increases in glycine can occasionally occur in mitochondrial disorders due to impaired lipoate cofactor assembly, but primary glycine encephalopathy typically displays an abnormally high CSF-to-plasma glycine ratio (greater than 0.08-0.10). Establishing that the ratio remains normal in MMDS9B provides an actionable clinical rule-out tool.

evidence.text: The diagnostic hallmark of nonketotic hyperglycinemia (NKH) is not merely absolute glycine elevation, but an elevated CSF-to-plasma glycine ratio (e.g., 0.19 in reported neonatal NKH).

new_directions.question_text: In patients with biallelic FDXR mutations who present with isolated optic-acoustic neuropathy versus infantile Leigh-like syndrome, what is the exact quantitative distribution of CSF-to-plasma glycine ratios and blood lactate levels?
new_directions.rationale: Clarifying whether the CSF/plasma glycine ratio is strictly <0.04 in juvenile-onset MMDS9B patients will establish whether classic nonketotic hyperglycinemia workup definitively excludes MMDS9B.

new_directions.question_text: Do urine organic acid profiles in FDXR deficiency consistently demonstrate secondary markers of lipoate deficiency, such as elevated 2-ketoglutarate and 2-hydroxybutyrate, or are they entirely normal in older patients?
new_directions.rationale: Lipoate-dependent enzyme dysfunction characteristically drives the biochemical abnormalities in MMDS1-3; confirming whether MMDS9B shows subtle urine organic acid lipoate signatures would clarify its enzymatic pathogenesis.
